", "full_text": "How 3 Java Champions are using GitHub Copilot for increased productivity - The GitHub Blog Julien Dubois · @jdubois October 20, 2026 | 17 minutes Share: AI coding tools can generate code quickly, but speed alone does not solve the hardest software engineering problems. Developers still need to provide context, validate results, protect maintainability, and remain accountable for what ships. To learn how experienced developers strike that balance, we spoke with three Java Champions, all with over a decade of experience in using Java. They shared concrete examples of using GitHub Copilot in production and open source, along with the practices they use to turn AI-generated output into reliable software. Here are the tips they shared with us. Vlad Mihalcea GitHub profile: @vladmihalcea How has GitHub Copilot helped you recently? I’ve been using it to analyze, design, and implement various features in both Hypersistence Utils and Hypersistence Optimizer. For example, I’ve been wanting for a long time to develop a web application that provides Optimizer event history so we can see how performance improvement efforts are materializing in application performance. Before AI, I kept postponing this task because it would have taken me weeks to develop. But using Copilot is like having a new team member, so I used it to create an app that will ship in the next version of Hypersistence Optimizer. Instead of weeks, this task took just two days to implement. What’s your typical usage? Are you using GitHub Copilot as an IDE plugin or the GitHub Copilot app? I use GitHub Copilot in IntelliJ IDEA because it’s convenient to run while reviewing source code or during a debug session. It’s very useful as a code assistant, and it helps me speed up both investigations and building prototypes for features that need validation. I still review the plans and the code that is generated by AI since their goal is to improve my productivity, not replace me entirely. While AI provides the right answer in many situations, there are still times when the response is not satisfactory and requires my intervention. Can you share some tips and best practices? For example, which skills are you using? I created my own skills so that whatever text Copilot generates looks like something I wrote by hand. This skill captures my voice from 65 of my published articles, so a draft comes back sounding like my blog instead of like a language model. This is really useful when generating documentation for this project, since it lets the LLM learn from 12 years of blogging and provide examples that follow the same principles, such as expressiveness, testability, and simplicity. Throughout my career as a software engineer, I’ve learned that we spend far more time on code maintenance than on creating it. Therefore, because maintenance and stability are critical for existing products, I developed skills that help AI mimic existing code practices in accordance with the principle of least astonishment. One tip is to change the model type based on the type of operation. For thorough thinking, I use Opus with the 1 million context window and Extra High or Max reasoning. However, for simpler tasks, such as generating reports, release notes, or verifying documentation, I use lighter models that consume fewer tokens. Patrick Baumgartner GitHub profile: @patbaumgartner Your work involves coaching teams. What is your approach? A lot of my work happens while the normal business still has to keep running. You cannot stop everything for six months to “transform.” We usually start by solving immediate problems together, understand where the team currently stands, define where we want to go and how we will know that we are improving, and then move there step by step. Depending on the situation, that can mean Software Craft practices such as TDD, refactoring, continuous delivery and XP; architecture and modularisation with Spring Boot, Spring Modulith; Spring Security; optimising Java and Spring Boot applications for containers; or increasingly, agentic engineering. The important part for me is that I work with the team. We make decisions together. I don’t want a team to become dependent on me. Ideally, after some time they no longer need me except perhaps as a sparring partner. And maybe that explains why I find this new generation of AI tools so interesting: I like working with people, learning, experimenting, and solving problems. AI gives us another very powerful tool for doing exactly that. Can you share a good story about how GitHub Copilot has helped you recently? There are actually three very different examples that changed how I think about working with GitHub Copilot. Let’s start with the first one. One was a migration of around 900 teaching slides across 15 presentations from Reveal.js to Marp. These were not simple slides. Many contain code, animations, and even interactive examples where I can change JavaScript live while teaching. More importantly, the presentations had already been battle-tested with students. The flow worked. Losing one small piece could break the story I use in the classroom. Doing that migration manually would probably have taken me a week or more—and realistically, I might simply have avoided doing it because it was such tedious work. With Copilot, I approached it differently. We first analysed the existing material, defined the target, created a migration plan, established constraints, provided examples, and defined what had to remain intact. Then we worked from the big structural changes down into the details. The really important part was verification. We generated screenshots of the Reveal.js and Marp versions and compared them visually and algorithmically. We built a small application where I could run both slide decks next to each other to verify animations manually. We even compared the generated PDFs. That meant the agent did not just say, “Migration complete.” We had evidence. The entire migration took me roughly eight to ten hours. I still owned the content, the teaching intent, and every meaningful change. Copilot could fix a typo automatically, but if content, versions, dates or meaning changed, that was something we discussed. For me, that experience reinforced an important principle: delegate execution, not responsibility. I own the result. Can you share the second example? A second example came from building a terminal UI application with Tamboui. It initially worked perfectly in Linux under WSL, and I had completely forgotten that somebody might run it directly in Windows CMD or PowerShell. And then a real user did. They discovered that the Enter key was simply ignored in some forms. That is another principle I strongly believe in: ship software early, because you learn from how people actually use it. We used Copilot to turn that feedback into reproducible UI tests. On Linux, Copilot was navigating the application with tmux. Through working with it, I learned about psmux and could execute similar flows in PowerShell. We reproduced the problem, created a local fix, traced the real problem into Tamboui, and I submitted the upstream fix, which was merged. During this work, the test descriptions themselves became too large for the available context. So I asked Copilot to help me redesign the way the tests were represented. Instead of verbose tables containing identifiers, names and repeated descriptions, it proposed a much more compact arrow notation: step → step → input, with additional information only where it was critical. That surprised me. We were not just using AI to execute information; we were working together on how information should be represented for execution . It did not have to be maximally human-friendly. It had to preserve the semantics while being efficient for the agent. How about the third example? The third example is completely different again. Someone close to me needed to practise mathematics, and I thought: why don’t we build a small learning app? It covers addition, subtraction, multiplication, division and division with remainder for grades one through four. But I did not want to build another simple quiz application. Together with Copilot, I researched learning approaches such as spaced repetition, immediate feedback, adaptive difficulty, motivation, cooperative learning and gamification without dark patterns. Interestingly, during that research Copilot challenged one of my original assumptions. I initially wanted the application to be generic for children everywhere. The research led us toward looking at the actual school curriculum instead. I realised that the order in which topics are introduced, the operations and number ranges differ enough that making it “universal” immediately was unnecessary. So we focused on Switzerland first and aligned the progression accordingly. Because Switzerland is multilingual, the application is available in German, French, Italian and English. It also has cooperative and competitive two-player modes, and when someone gets an answer wrong, the application explains one way to solve it and brings similar questions back through spaced repetition. I deliberately chose an architecture without a backend. There is no reason for me to collect children’s personal data on a server, so the data stays on the device and the application can simply be hosted on GitHub Pages. What started as a small experiment is now being used and shared among friends. It accidentally became a little product. That experience showed me another side of Copilot: don’t only use it to implement your solution. Use it as a sparring partner to expand and challenge the solution space before you start building . How do you typically use Copilot? I actually don’t use the classic Copilot autocomplete experience anymore. My work has moved almost completely toward agentic workflows. I use VS Code when I need a tight visual feedback loop—when I want to look closely at documents, code, presentations or intermediate results and adapt the process as I go. For larger execution-oriented tasks, I often work with the coding agent from the terminal. There I am more comfortable delegating a piece of work, letting it execute, and then inspecting the complete result. The interface I choose depends mostly on the feedback loop I need. I also had a fascinating experience using the coding-agent workflow through GitHub while travelling to JavaLand. I had started exploring an idea for a Maven plugin that optimises which Spring Boot auto-configurations are loaded. During roughly a four-hour journey, I was steering the agent from my phone: giving it a task, reviewing what it had done, thinking about the next step, and sending the next instruction. By the time I arrived, I had a working Maven plugin, a CI pipeline, performance tests against a sample application, and reports that could demonstrate whether the optimisation actually worked. That was the first time I had worked that way, and I was amazed that it actually worked. I wasn’t trying to write Java on my phone. I was reviewing, deciding and steering while the agent executed . I also use MCP servers when they give me useful capabilities or context. For example, I have used Context7 for documentation, integrations with my Logseq knowledge base, and I have experimented with an MCP integration for Adobe Premiere Pro. But I don’t use MCP just because I can. If a good CLI exists, I often prefer the CLI because it feels more direct and faster to me. The agent is also not a “junior developer” in my mental model. I think of it much more as a sparring partner. But just like anyone joining a project, it first needs to be brought up to speed. Context is king. Can you share some tips and best practices? The biggest thing I would recommend is: stop one-shot prompting. For anything non-trivial, I want to understand the problem before execution starts. Quite often I explicitly ask the agent to interview me first. The purpose of that interview is to uncover assumptions and expectations that are still implicit. A good agent can execute the wrong idea incredibly quickly. That does not make the detour cheaper. I experienced this myself while working on my Spring Boot auto-configuration optimiser. Initially I wanted to support both Spring Boot 3.5 and 4.x. There were architectural differences, so we implemented both approaches. Later I realised I no longer needed the 3.5 path and removing it was painful. The lesson was simple: detours are expensive. Get the requirements right before you accelerate. Once the intent is clear, I want a plan. When I review that plan, four things matter especially to me: are assumptions visible, are verification gates defined, does the approach fit the architecture, and does it avoid unnecessary work? The second principle is to define task-specific verification gates. “Done” should not mean that the model says it is done. For a refactoring, the gates might include passing tests, proving that all intended files were handled, updating documentation and leaving no TODOs behind. For the slide migration, the gates included screenshots, visual diffs, animations, PDF output and content completeness. The gates depend on the task. The principle does not: the agent should be able to provide evidence that the work satisfies the definition of done. I recently came across a skill called unlazy that follows a similar idea: create explicit gates, work through them deliberately, and prove that they have been completed rather than taking shortcuts. The third principle is to turn your lessons into reusable skills . I have started writing and maintaining my own Agent Skills. When I learn something from an execution—perhaps the agent misunderstood a convention, a useful check was missing, or I found a better way to approach a task—I update the skill. The next time I perform that task, the lesson is already there. One example is a skill I call maintainer-audit , inspired by work in the open agent skills community. I use it across my own repositories. It checks and, where appropriate, fixes the things I expect a maintained project to have: repository documentation, CI pipelines, Dependabot configuration, CodeQL, consistent cleanup and other project standards. The goal is not to generate another audit report for me to read. It brings the repository back toward the baseline I want automatically. That makes my projects more consistent and easier to maintain. I think of these skills as living engineering knowledge rather than static prompts. The fourth principle is to put deterministic engineering tools around the probabilistic model. I have my own quality harness that wraps tools such as Checkstyle, PMD and Spring Modulith architecture checks and produces a consolidated report that the agent can consume. I can run that from hooks and let the agent iterate: change → execute checks → read findings → fix → execute again. It continues until there are no findings left. That does not mean I stop looking at the software. I still run the application, interact with it and decide whether it behaves and looks the way I expect. Sometimes I deliberately implement feature by feature because the feedback loop is much tighter. I learned that asking for everything at once because “the AI can do it” is usually a bad idea. Large, generic specifications create large, generic implementations—and cleaning them up afterwards can be harder than building smaller increments correctly. More broadly, I think we developers need to talk much more about how we use these tools. Share the experiments that worked. Share the ones that didn’t. Borrow ideas from each other and adapt them to your own context instead of looking for one universal AI development process. That is also why I like the idea of AI as a sparring partner. On a Friday night, when I want to experiment with something and no human pair is available, I suddenly have somebody—or something—I can challenge an idea with, review an approach with, or use as a very sophisticated rubber duck. But I still take those ideas back to real people. Human feedback, product understanding and real-world context remain essential. How do you think AI is changing our profession? I don’t think software engineering students should primarily aspire to become code-producing machines. They need to become strong problem solvers. They need to understand users and stakeholders, discover the real problem behind a requirement, challenge assumptions, understand products and markets, make architectural trade-offs, think critically, work in a structured way and transfer useful solutions from one context into another. The model is extraordinarily good at generating possibilities and executing things. But as a human, I usually know much more of the actual context—including the things nobody ever documented. So I want to remain in charge of shaping the solution and let the agent take over more of the execution. In that sense, I think AI is putting the engineering back into software engineering . And I like that. Frank Delporte GitHub profile: @FDelporte How did you get started in tech? I’ve been fascinated by computers since I got a Commodore 64 when I was 11. Took some side steps into video production and television work after school but turned back into coding as that video needed to be put on DVD and the very first websites… Yes, I’m that old ;-). How has GitHub Copilot helped you recently? It’s a perfect companion to evaluate pull requests and investigate bug reports. One remarkable story is about the Pi4J library that lets you build Java applications to interact with electronic components on the Raspberry Pi. In February 2026, we released V4 which has a new plugin using the Foreign Function & Memory API. We tested it thoroughly before releasing, but still, shortly after the release someone reported that using 5 input buttons doesn’t work as expected . Pushing one of the first four configured buttons triggers a code execution as expected, while nothing happens with the fifth button. This is the kind of report you don’t want to get. Nothing was visibly broken. No exception, no warning in the logs, the fifth button was simply silent. And it got worse: with the older gpiod plugin, the exact same hardware and the exact same application, worked fine. So the problem was in our new FFM code, which sits on top of the Linux kernel’s GPIO character device and talks to it through native calls. That is not the part of the codebase where you expect to find a quick answer. So I assigned the issue to the Copilot coding agent and gave it two file paths as a starting point, the provider class and FFMDigitalInput. About half an hour later there was a pull request, with an explanation I really did not expect. Each input runs an event watcher that blocks in a native poll() call, waiting for the kernel to report a change on its GPIO line. Those watchers ran in virtual threads. And a virtual thread that blocks inside a native call cannot be unmounted from its carrier thread. It stays pinned there for the whole duration of the call. A Raspberry Pi 4 has four cores, so the virtual thread scheduler has four carrier threads. Register four inputs, and all four carriers are parked in poll() forever. The fifth watcher is created, but is never scheduled. That is exactly the bug that was reported. Not “events are flaky”, but “the fifth one does nothing.” What I liked most was not the diff, it was the conversation that followed in the review. I left a comment asking Copilot to explain this in more detail: I thought the goal of virtual threads was exactly to step away from the platform thread limit? So how is this a problem that four virtual threads block the four threads on a four-core processor like the Raspberry Pi? Check the pull request for the full conversation . Copilot was able to link the use of the Raspberry Pi which has four CPU cores with the reported problem. It was able to propose a simple fix for the problem, plus some extra improvements it found during its investigation. Can you share some tips and best practices? Tell it where to look: For the Pi4J issue #622, I added two file paths. That is a tiny bit of effort that removes a huge amount of searching in a large codebase. You usually have a hunch about the neighbourhood even when you have no idea about the bug. Give it to the tool so it doesn’t need to investigate the complete code. Ask for proof and tests: “Add a unit test to validate the change” is something I ask a lot these days. Well, asked, because it has now become a rule in my instructions file. It also prevents cases where the diagnosis was wrong, because the test won’t fail on the old code. Ask why: If you don’t understand a fix, say so and ask. The explanation is a deliverable too and should be added into your project documentation or inside the ticket or pull request. It teaches everyone who reads the info later. For example, this also triggered more questions within the Pi4J team about virtual thread pinning on native calls. Stay in control: All of these pull requests in Pi4J were reviewed and approved by maintainers before they went in. That’s the model that works best in this project: the agent does the investigation, the humans stay responsible for what ships. But also for my other projects I always do a review of the code that was generated by the tool. I always want to keep code readable and maintainable. Too often, a tool creates duplicate methods or recreates something which is already available in another place and should be combined. That’s your responsibility. You can go very fast these days with AI-assisted coding, which also means you can very fast create a mess. Don’t do that, keep your code manageable, your colleagues and future-self will thank you if they have to investigate bugs or make improvements later. concatenation and substitution Use the right per-codebase test framework This document is a style guide for the usage of the Rust programming language at Google. In this context, “style” refers to more than just formatting; it includes guidance on API and implementation design. Rust is used in many places, including google3 , Android, ChromeOS, Fuchsia, and Chrome, and we’d like for Rust usage at Google to be consistent both within and across codebases. In addition to bringing consistency to our Rust code, style guidance also helps establish a standard of quality. Background Scope The current scope of authority of the rules outlined in this guide: In Android, Chromium, and other codebases : This style guide has been developed in consultation with other codebases, and they intend to start applying it. These codebases may have their own rules about how strictly this is expected to be applied. Expect more information here as these codebases adopt this guide. Goals of the style guide By and large, we have this document for the same reasons we have a C++ style guide . Most style rules come from one or more of the goals listed below. Style rules should prioritize readability and maintainability over writeability We expect our code to be around for long periods of time, and we consider a little bit of extra effort applied during code writing to be worth it in the long run if the style rule improves readability. Style rules should favor better automation Large-Scale Changes (LSCs) are common at Google, and consistency helps make LSCs easier to carry out. Style rules should be consistent with the wider Rust ecosystem where possible The broader Rust ecosystem already has a pretty good amount of consistency in style, and we should rely on that where possible to reduce surprise and make it less work to learn Google’s Rust style. Style rules should pull their weight Every Rust developer and reviewer at Google has to keep these style rules in mind: as such, we should be careful to include rules that have a tangible benefit. Style rules may help avoid minor style disagreements There are many cases where reasonable people may disagree about a style, and we expect that disagreement to show up often on CLs. Having a style rule helps avoid having to rehash this each time. Rules in this category that do not have other benefits should be kept to a minimum. Follow public Rust style rules Follow the official public Rust style rules to the extent they don’t conflict with this style guide. Rust Style Guide Most code formatting conventions are enforced automatically by rustfmt. Rust API Guidelines A “conflict” would be a case where this style guide suggests a pattern that is discouraged, or counter to the primary encouraged pattern in the Rust style guide. Why does the guidance in this style guide deviate from regular Rust style rules? Most style guides have three goals: consistency, readability, and encouraging good API design. Regardless of the specific choices made, it helps everyone to have these choices made beforehand to limit bikeshedding. This style guide shares those goals, but it also has an additional goal not seen as often: smoothing the way for Large-Scale Changes (LSCs). Large codebases like many of the ones at Google occasionally need to run codebase-spanning refactorings that are assisted by tooling: for this to work well, the code should be something tooling has an easy time working with. Consistency helps for this, but so does having deliberate refactor-friendly patterns. Apply API design rules in context When applying rules that relate to API design, you should distinguish two types of code: Library code Intended for use by other projects (applications or other libraries). Solves a relatively general problem. Application code Intended for use in a single application. Solves a more specific problem. For library code , style guide rules that concern API design are binding. For application code , the rules on API design are a strong recommendation. As you apply them, keep in mind that since application code is written to solve a specific problem, it should generally favor simplicity and directness over broad reusability. Avoid premature generalization and abstraction; focus on what is required to meet the immediate need. Code organization Terminology: A crate is a unit of compilation. A crate always contains a nameless Rust module, the “root module”. A Rust module is a unit of code organization within a crate. Rust modules are used to control visibility of names. Modules can be nested. They can also be used to split code across files and directories. The following sections convey that in Chromium, it is preferable to not make use of all possibilities of splitting modules across files. Prefer small crates [chrome] Prefer small crates in Chromium; ideally, but not necessarily, a single file (focusing on one abstraction). If your code can be split up into small crates, do so. A crate corresponds to a single rust_static_library (chrome) rule, which may contain one or more .rs files. Additional considerations: The root module is allowed to re-export public APIs from leaf submodules , making submodules an implementation detail of the crate (as users don’t need to know about these submodules). This rule about small crates applies equally to crates with and without submodules. First, evaluate whether the APIs need to be in the same crate, and only then consider whether submodules could help organize the APIs. If you decide to use submodules, follow the expected file structure . Larger crates are allowed when trait impl coherence rules force multiple types and traits to be included in one library, or if you’re building a large foundational library. Rationale Fine-grained library targets are recommended in Chromium due to the massive size of our codebase, non-local effects of adding dependencies in the build graph, and to improve performance of parallel compilation and build caching. Use flat file layout for rust_library sources [chrome] In Chromium .rs source files belonging to one rust_library (one Rust crate) must reside in a single directory. Don’t use subdirectories to organize files that belong to a single crate. If organizing one crate’s files into subdirectories feels necessary, this is a strong indication that the crate has grown too large and should be split. This crate layout is intentionally different from the conventional Cargo directory structure typically used in open-source repositories. Exception: Rust code in //third_party that is also built with Cargo should follow the conventional Cargo directory structure. Rationale The approach in Chromium is driven by the following factors: Based on the preference for small crates , most rust_library targets will only contain one source file. Because of the above point, creating a directory for each rust_library target would result in most directories containing only one source file. Multi-file rust_library targets should not create dedicated directories for submodules either; this ensures a consistent approach. Name source files and leaf modules after the primary user-defined item When a leaf module has a primary user-defined item (e.g., Foo ), the module should be named after that item (e.g., mod foo and foo.rs ). Leaf modules that are not primarily about any particular abstraction can be named as desired. Rationale This makes it easy to identify the content/purpose of a source file or leaf module at a glance. Don’t implement APIs in non-leaf modules The only items in non-leaf modules should be module declarations (not definitions) and re-exports . Note that the definition of leaf modules allows the following sub-modules: mod test and cross-language binding modules like #[cxx::bridge] . Exceptions: Having a small amount of core “ties things together” implementation code in a non-leaf module may be fine. The goal is to not have a lot of code in these modules. Rationale This makes it easier to find things, and avoids mixing structure and contents. Don’t use glob imports Don’t use glob imports, except in the following situations where you may optionally do so at your own discretion: use super::* for inline modules use enum::* in method bodies of enums, and functions that are primarily dealing with that enum pub use submodule::* for non-leaf modules C++ interop: Since the same namespace (in C++) is a submodule in different Rust crates (in Rust), you may merge the namespaces into a private copy using glob imports. For example: mod absl { pub use status :: absl :: * ; pub use strings :: absl :: * ; } In this hypothetical example, you can use absl::Status and absl::StrCat from Rust, the same way you would from C++, instead of spelling them as status::absl::Status and strings::absl::StrCat . This must only be used for merging C++ namespaces, and the resulting merged module must not be public. If using third-party crates that encourage a prelude, it is up to the reviewer’s discretion to allow it. This also means that defining preludes should be avoided. Rationale Glob imports increase toil for code janitors running LSCs, and make it harder to know where a type comes from in contexts without xrefs. A use statement should import items from one module This rule corresponds to the rustfmt setting imports_granularity = Module . Basically, there should not be any :: ’s inside the {..} block of a use statement. For example: use foo :: Foo ; use foo :: bar :: Bar ; use foo :: bar :: Baz ; use foo :: Foo ; use foo :: bar ::{ Bar , Baz }; use foo ::{ Foo , bar :: Bar }; Prefer locally-scoped trait imports Import traits within function bodies, unless the trait’s methods are used extensively throughout the file. fn foo ( x : u8 ) { // Import the trait within a function, not at the module scope. use std :: str :: FromStr ; let string : String = x .parse (); } Qualify calls to top-level functions with a module name To use top-level functions defined in other modules or crates, import their module and call them with modulename::functionname() . For example: use std :: mem ; let x = mem :: transmute ( y ); use std :: mem :: transmute ; let x = transmute ( y ); Exceptions: When importing functions with sufficiently disambiguated names, e.g., functions from C++ (where it is typical to call top-level (free) functions directly). In Chromium, when importing functions from small, single-purpose first-party crates . When the module name itself is prone to collisions. For example, when the module name is a C++ namespace name, and multiple crates define the same submodules. Rationale Many Rust codebases consistently keep a style such that unqualified lowercase names are assumed local, so foo() can be assumed to be from the same module. This rule largely exists to avoid reviewer disagreements, the benefit is mostly consistency and a minor edge on reading code without xrefs. Type names should be imported and used unqualified By default, types and traits should be referenced in code without using their module path, e.g., code should use Regex , not regex::Regex , with a use regex::Regex at the top of the file or potentially in the relevant function. Exceptions: In cases where there are ambiguities, it is acceptable to directly reference types with common names like io::Error . It is also acceptable to rename ( use std::io::Error as IoError ). In cases where you have a large “group” of types, e.g. the hir module in rustc which contains a large number of HIR types. In macros and generated code; where requiring a use is counterproductive. In code with lots of dependencies, where importing everything would lead to a very large import block with little benefit. Rationale This rule largely exists to avoid reviewer disagreements. Use the appropriate import mechanism [chrome] Chrome Use chromium::import!() . Code formatting and aesthetics Use the appropriate formatting tool Use the appropriate formatting tool (e.g., git cl format in Chromium). Configuration (for style guide authors) A codebase may choose to not apply the following rustfmt options if they care about building on stable and the option is unavailable on their stable Rust: Maximum of 100 columns per line: max_width = 100 Usage of lowercase alphabets in hex literals ( 0xab123cdef as opposed to 0xAB123CDEF ): hex_literal_case = Lower Macro matcher formatting: format_macro_matchers = true Usage of escapes for invisible characters in literals. E.g., if you wish to have text containing a Zero-Width joiner, use \\u{200D} . Opting out of automatic formatting You may opt out of automatic formatting using #[rustfmt::skip] , but only in the following situations: Manual alignment – If you have a situation-specific reason to have a snippet of code line up in a particular way (e.g., multiple similar lines of code that you want to remain aligned for readability, or a matrix-constructing function). Generated code (ideally, use a genrule instead). Important: Formatting should not be skipped for personal style choices. Ownership and borrowing Avoid Rc and Arc Prefer unique ownership and borrowing over Rc and Arc for managing memory. Exception: Use Rc and Arc when the alternative ownership and borrowing structure would be unreasonably complex to write, understand, or maintain. This is a judgment call to be discussed during code review. Rationale Generally, Rust allows representing object graphs without using shared ownership smart pointers. These pointers add runtime overhead and their own unique complexity. Engineers coming from other languages might tend to use Rc and Arc too quickly. Prefer borrows over deep copies Use .clone() when you genuinely need a deep copy of an object. Avoid using .clone() as a substitute for borrowing. Design code that works naturally with Rust’s ownership and borrowing rules. However, if the borrowing relationships become excessively complex, .clone() can be a pragmatic choice. Consider the performance needs of the code while choosing between cloning and borrowing. Note: This advice does not apply to cloning Rc or Arc pointers. Cloning reference-counted pointers does not create a deep copy, and is an expected way to use them. Rationale Deep copies can be expensive to make due to memory allocation and data copying. Function inputs and outputs Accept flexible references for immutable data When functions accept borrowed, immutable data, use a reference type that affords the most flexibility. Pass references to the data itself instead of references to smart pointers, containers, or wrappers. Use Instead of Why? &T &Box Borrow the data inside the box &[T] &Vec Accept any slice instead of specific containers &str &String Accept a string slice instead of references to owned strings Option<&T> &Option Borrow the data inside the Option Exceptions: When expecting non-linear character data such as Rope/Cord. For context, see Clippy lints borrowed_box and ptr_arg . Rationale Accepting reference types that don’t mention specific smart pointers, containers, or wrappers makes functions more versatile and performant: callers can pass data held in a variety of ways without copying it first. Iterators vs. owned collections in return types Prefer returning iterators (either concrete types or impl Iterator ) where possible over returning Vec . Note: In application code, returning a Vec is fine if it simplifies the code and if flexibility and performance advantages of iterators are not clearly needed. Exceptions: Most callers will need to construct an owned vector. The function’s implementation naturally constructs a vector. The returned value will likely need to be randomly indexed. The algorithm works better as a for loop and the forced allocation doesn’t matter too much. The function’s intended purpose is creating a new owned collection. The function is returning a pre-existing vector. Rationale Highly reusable library code generally should strive to provide more flexible and performant APIs. Returning an iterator allows callers to choose how to consume the data: collect it into a vector, process it in a loop, or chain further iterator adapters. Some of these options allow users to avoid unnecessary allocations. In application code, the usage patterns for a function are often easier to predict. If it is clear that performance is not a concern, or that data would be collected into a vector anyway, returning a vector makes for a simpler API. Iterators vs. slices in function parameters Highly reusable library code should accept iterators or impl IntoIterator if it only needs to iterate over the input. Note: In application code, accepting a slice &[T] is fine if it simplifies the code and if flexibility and performance advantages of iterators are not clearly needed. Rationale Highly reusable library code generally should strive to provide more flexible and performant APIs. Functions that accept iterators offer callers: More flexibility (data can be supplied from any collection) Efficiency (data does not need to be copied into a contiguous piece of memory) Composability (the function works better with iterator chains) In application code, the usage patterns for a function are often easier to predict. If it is clear that performance is not a concern, or that callers would always have a vector anyway, accepting a slice makes for a simpler API. Accepting Into When designing library APIs that accept a T but users are likely to have various types, consider accepting impl Into instead of T if call-site ergonomics are paramount . Tip: This should be balanced against code bloat concerns; it is not a requirement to use lots of Into in your code. Note: Application code should almost never use impl Into parameters. Rationale Using impl Into allows a function to directly accept various arguments of various compatible types. For example, a function accepting impl Into could be called with a String or a &str literal directly. The tradeoff here is balancing the convenience of avoiding a .into() at the callsite against the cost of generics (more complex API signature, increased code size, sometimes even type inference difficulties). Prefer enum over bool in APIs Use enum function parameters instead of bool in cases where the purpose of the parameter is not obvious. If you do use bool , consider using an inline comment to document the purpose of the bool in an argument list. Reporting errors Choose the error reporting mechanism that fits your API contract: Option , Result , or panic! . Use Option for simple failures where the cause is obvious and the caller would not benefit from further details. This is best for standard, anticipated outcomes like a missing value or a parsing mismatch. // Good: The cause of the failure is obvious (integer overflow). No further // details could be reasonably provided. fn checked_add ( a : u32 , b : u32 ) -> Option < u32 > { ... } Use Result for recoverable failures where the caller needs context to handle the error. These are often “unavoidable” errors caused by external factors (like I/O or network) that even correctly implemented code cannot prevent with checks ahead of time. Nevertheless, the caller can reasonably anticipate the kinds of errors (a file-related function can fail with an I/O error). The error details allow the caller to distinguish failure modes and recover appropriately. // Good: The caller needs to know *why* it failed (NotFound vs PermissionDenied). fn open_file ( path : & Path ) -> Result < File , io :: Error > { ... } Use panic! to report bugs and violated invariants. These errors are avoidable: the program is missing a check, and is calling an operation without fulfilling a precondition. These defects must be fixed in the code, not handled at runtime, although coarse-grained recovery might be possible with catch_unwind . // Good: Panics if the invariant (index must be in bounds) is violated. // This indicates a bug in the caller's logic. impl < T > MyVec < T > { pub fn remove ( & mut self , index : usize ) -> T { if index >= self .len () { panic! ( \"index out of bounds\" ); } // ... } } Note: Some codebases may choose to avoid panics entirely, and require even broken invariants to be reported via Result . Exceptions: Developer-facing binaries may use panics for non-fatal errors. Tests may use panics for assertions. Types Newtypes versus type aliases Use a newtype instead of a type alias in the following cases: If the type you are defining has notable semantic differences. For types that warrant an API of their own. If you want the flexibility to change the underlying type later, especially if you don’t control all usages of your type. For type safety, if it’s easy for the types to get mixed up. For example, a Date type may use newtypes to distinguish Day , Month , and Year numbers in its internal calculations. Prefer named fields over tuples and non-newtype tuple structs Prefer types with named fields over tuples, as tuple indexes ( .0 , .1 , …) quickly become confusing. Exceptions: Newtype tuple structs (tuple structs with only one field). In very local contexts where there is unlikely to be any confusion. Traits Add trait implementations when they become necessary As a general rule, low-level library code should anticipate users’ needs proactively, while application code should add trait impls as needed. Implement known standard library traits instead of custom methods If a method matches the purpose and behavior of a standard library trait, implement that trait. For example, instead of writing fn from_str(&str) -> Self on Foo , you should impl FromStr for Foo . It is acceptable to have both the method and the trait impl for discoverability reasons. For context, see Clippy lint should_implement_trait ( list of traits ). Use #[derive()] if possible Manual implementations should be avoided if they can be expressed as a #[derive()] . Generics versus dyn Trait In libraries, prefer accepting generics ( T: Trait or impl Trait ) in function parameters over dyn Trait . Exceptions: Cases where code size matters. Rationale Efficiency Additional indirection: Creating a dyn Trait requires setting up a fat pointer, and a vtable lookup is required for every call of a function on the trait. If a function takes a dyn Trait , the compiler can’t perform certain optimizations that it could if the function was generic, such as inlining calls to functions of the trait. Some traits are not dyn compatible . For example, a trait is not dyn compatible if it has generic functions, associated functions without a self parameter, or functions that return Self . When to define a trait versus an inherent implementation Define a trait only for the following purposes: To enable generic programming (to use T: Trait in constraints of generic functions and types). To accept or return an impl Trait or dyn Trait . To define an extension trait (but see also the caveats in the section on extension traits). In all other cases where you want to implement functionality for a type, use an inherent implementation . Don’t use traits merely to organize code. Extension traits An extension trait is a trait that adds methods to a type from a different crate. What differentiates an extension trait from other traits is that its sole purpose is to add methods to the type; it is not intended for use in generics ( T: Trait , impl Trait ) or dynamic dispatch ( dyn Trait ). To indicate this, the name of an extension trait should carry the suffix ~Ext (for example, ForeignTypeExt ). In general, the team that owns the original type should also own the extension trait. Exceptions: Extension methods that are expected to become well known and provide significant value, for example, in foundational libraries / frameworks. Note: This rule is specifically about extension traits. It is relatively common to define a trait as an input trait (e.g., DateLike ) and implement it on a bunch of foreign types. Examples extern crate foreign_crate ; use foreign_crate :: ForeignType ; trait ForeignTypeExt { fn additional_method ( & self ); } impl ForeignTypeExt for ForeignType { fn additional_method ( & self ) { ... } } It is also possible to define an extension trait for every type that implements some foreign trait. Effectively, this is equivalent to adding default methods to the foreign trait: extern crate foreign_crate ; use foreign_crate :: ForeignTrait ; trait ForeignTraitExt { fn additional_method ( & self ); } impl < T : ForeignTrait > ForeignTraitExt for T { fn additional_method ( & self ) { ... } } Rationale When the same team owns the extension trait and the type being extended, this helps avoid method name conflicts between the base type and the extension trait or between two extension traits. Specific guidance for important traits Types with public fields : Consider implementing traits implemented by all subfields. Error types : Implement the Copy trait whenever possible. Copy types are simpler to manage and propagate because they can be passed by value without moving ownership. An example of a case where this is not possible is if the error must contain non- Copy fields like a String . Copy : Implement whenever it is reasonably clear that the type will continue to be Copy in the future. Clone : Most types should implement Clone unless they represent some external resource. Default : Implement if the type implements new() or otherwise has a default state. For context, see Clippy lint new_without_default . PartialEq / Eq : If you want users to use the == operator, prefer implementing PartialEq over Eq . When you do implement Eq , be aware of the additionally required reflexivity (details: https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/cmp/trait.Eq.html). PartialOrd / Ord : If you want users to use the < or > operators, prefer implementing PartialOrd over Ord . When you do implement Ord , be aware that it requires total ordering (details: https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/cmp/trait.Ord.html). Map keys If you think it is likely that a type will be used as a map key or otherwise cached, implement Hash and Eq . If, in addition, the type has a clear total ordering, implement Ord (and any traits it needs). Pair important From impls with explicit constructor methods If a type has an important From impl that is expected to be one of the primary ways of constructing it, add an inherent ::new() , ::new_from_foo() ¸ or ::from_foo() method. Options structs should implement Default Structs with all-public fields that are primarily used as a “bag of options” for a function should implement Default . Rationale This enables convenient use of struct update syntax ( Struct { a: 0, ..Default::default()} ). Concurrency Handling poison Never reach inside a poisoned mutex to get at its insides, no matter how tempting the use case may seem. Don’t use async / .await [chrome] Don’t use async / .await in Chromium. Don’t start new threads through the Rust standard library [chrome] In Chromium, prefer to use sequences instead of threads. Use fuchsia_sync::Mutex [Fuchsia] Use Fuchsia’s mutex type, rather than one from std::sync or parking_lot . Macros When considering how to express an API, prefer in order: Regular Rust functions, types, traits, objects, and modules. (Avoid macros, code generation, and metaprogramming where possible). macro_rules! -style macros. Other code generation strategies (e.g. genrule ) proc_macro macros. When you decide to use a macro or code generation, please weigh the benefits against the costs: IDEs, Code Search and other developer tools will work less well on code that uses macros. Macros can create dialects of the language that make it harder for engineers to work across the codebase. Large scale changes are more difficult and expensive to apply. Rationale Prefer non-macro facilities: Macros can create dialects of the language that make it harder for engineers to work across the codebase. When a reader sees a usage of a macro, they can make fewer assumptions about that code than if it didn’t use a macro. Macros are harder to write correctly than regular Rust code. Use macro_rules! for simple code generation: Since Rust macros operate on the AST, they can be less fragile than textual code generation. Naming Naming methods Follow the Rust standard library style for naming methods. See also the guidance on naming conventions in the Comprehensive Rust course. Specific considerations: Use prefixes such as as_...() , to_...() , or into_...() with the appropriate self convention. See also this section of the Rust API Guidelines and the Clippy lint wrong_self_convention . Naming lifetimes Lifetimes should have descriptive names, especially type lifetimes. Exceptions: Type lifetimes that are extremely generic abstractions like Cow . It is fine to use anonymous lifetimes ( '_ ) where they work. Single-character lifetimes are okay when they are simply expressing the relationship between a method’s input and output, or needed for a local higher-ranked lifetime bounds ( for<'a> ). Up to two such local lifetimes are fine, if more are needed, we strongly advise you to use descriptive names. Naming generic parameters Use a short name for your generic parameters (either single or multi character), related to the kind of thing they represent. Single-letter generics are okay, but the letter chosen should be somewhat indicative of the object type, ideally taken from the most important trait bound. T or U are fine when the generics are in a relatively unbound context; i.e. it is an API intended for use with most types, like Vec . Naming extension traits When naming an extension trait , give the name an ~Ext suffix (for example, ForeignTypeExt ). Naming initialization functions Follow these guidelines when naming initialization functions: Constructors: Use new() , or new_with_foo() if there is more than one. If the constructor returns a Result , use try_new() . Value-to-value conversions: Use from_foo() with an associated From impl. See here for details on when an operation can be considered to be a value-to-value conversion. Avoid abbreviations Don’t use abbreviations (especially acronyms and initialisms) that someone outside your project is unlikely to know. Don’t abbreviate by deleting letters within a word. See also the Google C++ Style Guide . Exceptions: Common abbreviations found in Wikipedia. Abbreviations that are unlikely to be confusing to people outside of your project, for example IpAddr . You and your reviewer should make this determination. In general, the preference should still be not to abbreviate. When and how to write documentation Add documentation comments to public APIs, potentially using the missing_doc lint to help with this. Best practices for documentation comments: Consider including examples: It is not necessary for every function to have examples, but enough functionality should be covered in examples somewhere to give an idea of how the crate works. Always document panic cases for functions which may panic due to malformed input. Clearly document invariants for unsafe functions and traits. Use capitalization and punctuation. Don’t explain the basics of the programming language. For example, don’t do the following: struct MockFileSystem { ... } /// A mock implementation of the FileSystem trait, intended to be used in unit tests. impl FileSystem for MockFileSystem Exceptions: Comments should say something that the code does not already say. If there’s nothing insightful to say, it is better to omit the comment than to repeat the function name in a trivial way. For example, don’t do the following (it’s fine to allow the lint in that case): /// Removes an element. pub fn remove_element () -> Element {} It is generally okay to omit documentation on individual enum variants, especially if their name is self-explanatory. How to format documentation comments Follow these guidelines when writing documentation comments: Use /// comments to document items following the comment, such as functions, structs, enums, traits, and type aliases. Use //! comments to document the module or the library itself. These comments should be placed at the top of the file. Follow the rules laid out in the official Rust style guide on doc comments . Use Markdown syntax. Use ordinary comment syntax ( // ) for non-documentation comments, such as implementation comments, TODOs that are not interesting for users, commented out source code, etc. Prefer to document things in a straightforward manner, using /// and //! comments, rather than generating documentation from macros. This makes the documentation directly readable when viewing or modifying the source code. It is acceptable, and even encouraged, to mix doc comments ( /// and //! ) and ordinary comments ( // ). If you have one thing you wish to document publicly, and another thing you want to note as an implementation comment, then use both! For example: /// Finds the first `FooItem` with the given `name`, or `None` if not present. // TODO: crbug.com/12345 - `name` should be &str, not String. pub fn get_named ( items : & [ FooItem ], name : String ) -> Option <& FooItem > { ... } Rationale Many, though not all, languages have a different commenting convention (such as extra * characters) for doc comments as opposed to implementation comments. Rust and Python are notable for not just having different commenting conventions, but an actual different syntax entirely. This has concrete benefits to the Rust ecosystem: Doc comments can be consumed by tooling, including documentation generators like rustdoc , IDE features, and Kythe. Doc comments have a standard structure and formatting rules (Markdown), allowing for rich text in those contexts. Errors in applying doc comment syntax (e.g., applying it to an expression instead of a documentable item) are linted against, catching documentation errors early. If there are no lint errors, the doc comments are guaranteed to be visible to documentation tooling, removing a degree of flakiness and unpredictability from the documentation process. Doc comments are a part of the AST, and so can be produced and consumed by macros, including both macro_rules! macros and procedural macros. Other Rust features Unsafe code Don’t write unsafe code unless there is no way to implement the same functionality with safe code. If you do have to write unsafe code: Encapsulate unsafe code in a safe abstraction and isolate it from business logic as much as possible. Ideally, unsafe code should be in a separate crate with few dependencies beyond the standard library. Add a safety comment starting with SAFETY: that explains why the code is correct. Add a technical justification for unsafe code. Depending on context, this can be a justification for an individual unsafe block or a more general justification that covers an entire file or build target. The justification should answer these questions: Why is this code not written in an equivalent safe way? If the reason is performance, are there benchmarks? No unstable features Don’t use unstable features. Exceptions: Android Embedded programming may require the use of certain unstable features. While review will be required to enable them (to help search for alternatives), features absolutely required to build an artifact correctly will generally be approved. Chrome Style arbiters may blanket-approve a small list of features for the entire codebase. Typically, only features that have a clear path to stabilization will be approved. Fuchsia See guidance here . Getters and setters Writing and naming getters and setters should follow these guidelines: foo() for a getter that returns a T by value. foo_mut() for a getter that returns a &mut T . take_foo() for a getter that “clears” the value (by setting it to None or some other default state) and returns the old value. set_foo() for a setter that takes a T by value. with_foo() / with_mut_foo() for an accessor that operates via a closure (see details below ). Such an accessor is invoked as object.with_foo(|foo| frob(foo)) . replace_foo() for a setter that returns the old value. Examples impl Stuff { fn foo ( & self ) -> & Foo { ... } fn foo_mut ( & mut self ) -> & mut Foo { ... } /// Sets \"baz\" property to `None` and returns the old value. fn take_baz ( & mut self ) -> Option < Baz > { ... } fn set_foo ( & mut self , foo : Foo ) { ... } /// Calls `f` with a borrow of the \"bar\" property. /// Returns the return value of `f`. fn with_bar < R > ( & self , f : impl FnOnce ( & Bar ) -> R ) -> R { ... } /// Calls `f` with a mutable borrow of the \"bar\" property. /// Returns the return value of `f`. fn with_mut_bar < R > ( & self , f : impl FnOnce ( & mut i32 ) -> R ) -> R { ... } /// Sets \"foo\" property to `foo` and returns the old value. fn replace_foo ( & mut self , foo : Foo ) -> Foo { ... } } More on accessors that accept closures Accessors that accept a closure ( .with_foo() ) are typically invoked as object.with_foo(|foo| do_something_with(foo)) . They can be a good choice in the following situations: When the property is contained in an interior mutability wrapper (e.g. Mutex or RefCell ). These mechanisms need to constrain access to the property to a scope, and the closure provides this scope. This is usually preferable to directly returning the RAII object that implements the scope (e.g. MutexGuard ) because the latter would leak an implementation detail. When follow-up work or validation is needed after a property is changed and a set_foo() accessor cannot be used (for example because the property’s type is expensive to clone or cannot be cloned at all). A with_foo() accessor will often allow the closure to return a value and forward it by returning it from with_foo() . If you need to provide two closure-accepting accessors, one for read-only access and one for mutable access, it is common to name them with_foo() and with_mut_foo() . Otherwise, with_foo() is often also used for mutating accessors. Implement expected API sets together If you implement len() , also implement is_empty() . For context, see Clippy lint len_without_is_empty . Do not access items marked #[doc(hidden)] that you don’t own Treat items marked #[doc(hidden)] as private. Don’t access them unless you own the code. Use const functions responsibly Mark a public function as const only if you expect it to remain const in the future (or can commit to helping clients migrate when it changes). Rationale It’s a breaking change to turn a const function into a regular function. Avoid overloading for non-mathematical purposes Use operator overloads for their original mathematical/logical purpose, not just to make the code more concise (as “syntax sugar”). Apply #[non_exhaustive] to publicly-exposed enums If an enum is part of a public API used by other teams, mark it #[non_exhaustive] . Exceptions: The enum will never change. For example: Enums describing an existing ontology (e.g., enum Color { Red, Green, Blue } ). Enums with two states that could be Booleans (e.g., enum Visibility { Visible, Hidden } ) The enum may change in the future, but you are committed to fixing resulting breakages via an LSC. For context, see Clippy lint exhaustive_enums . Rationale Marking an enum #[non_exhaustive] forces users to include a wildcard arm ( _ => ... ) in match statements. This ensures code continues to compile when new variants are added to the enum later. This rule is primarily important for enums used across team boundaries, because the scope of the breakage could be significant. Enums used only a small number of times can’t create a large breakage and thus may ignore this rule. Apply #[non_exhaustive] to public structs with public fields Structs with public fields that are part of a public API used by other teams should be marked #[non_exhaustive] . Exceptions: The struct fields are unlikely to change, e.g., because they describe an existing ontology (e.g., a Rectangle type) or the reviewer can otherwise be confident that they will not change. The struct fields may change in the future, but you are committed to fixing resulting breakages via an LSC. You want to enable your users to use functional record update (FRU) struct initialization syntax ( Person { name: \"foo\", ..Default::default() } ). Rationale Adding a new field (even a private one) to a struct with all public fields is a breaking change, because callers can no longer name all fields in a struct literal. A #[non_exhaustive] struct can’t be constructed with the struct literal syntax, except for the code in the same crate. This allows new private fields to be added without breaking users. This rule is primarily important for structs used across team boundaries, because the scope of the breakage could be significant. Structs used only a small number of times can’t create a large breakage and thus may ignore this rule. #[must_use] on functions Use #[must_use] on functions in these cases: The caller cannot use the function correctly if they ignore the return value. This includes pure functions (functions without side effects), such as HashMap::get() . Any function whose return value represents an error or otherwise critical information about the function’s behavior. If the return type is already annotated #[must_use] (which is true of Result , for example), the function does not need to be annotated #[must_use] . #[must_use] on types Use #[must_use] on types intended to be returned by functions that would otherwise be annotated #[must_use] according to the rules above . Examples: The type is an error type (similar to Result or StatusOr ). The type represents a lazily evaluated computation. In other words, the function call doesn’t do anything by itself, and the return value needs to be accessed to cause some desired side effect. Do not run code before main() Do not cause code to run before main() , for example by using techniques such as the ctor crate . Implementation concerns Don’t overuse type inference Add enough explicit types so that someone familiar with the codebase can figure out what the inferred types are. Prefer to add the types to variable declarations, rather than as turbofishes . If the compiler forces you to add a turbofish, it is generally fine to add a _ inference marker. Specific situations in which you should probably add types: When calling methods with a generic return type, such as .into() or .parse() . For the result of complex iterator chains. Prefer pattern matching over check-then-unwrap Avoid potentially panicking operations when the input data guarantees they cannot panic. For example, instead of using Option::unwrap on a value known to be valid, use pattern matching to prove correctness to the compiler. // Good: The match arm proves to the compiler that `x` is `Some`. // A panic is obviously not possible. if let Some ( value ) = option { use_value ( value ); } // Bad: Correctness of `unwrap` relies on a runtime check that `option` is `Some`. if option .is_some () { use_value ( option .unwrap ()); } Prefer expect over unwrap If a panic is necessary because an invariant cannot be expressed in the type system, prefer expect over unwrap to document the reason. Don’t omit patterns on non_exhaustive enums when matching Prefer to list all enum variants in match statements over non_exhaustive enums. If you don’t care about specific variants, place them in the wildcard arm. If you only care about specific variants, use an if let or a let … else {} . Examples: #[non_exhaustive] pub enum Shape { Circle , Square , Triangle , } fn process_shape ( shape : Shape ) { match shape { Shape :: Circle => println! ( \"It's a circle\" ), Shape :: Square => println! ( \"It's a square\" ), // Triangle and any future variants don't require any actions. Shape :: Triangle | _ => {} } } fn process_shape ( shape : Shape ) { if let Shape :: Circle = shape { println! ( \"It's a circle\" ), } } fn process_shape ( shape : Shape ) { match shape { Shape :: Circle => println! ( \"It's a circle\" ), _ => {} } } Exceptions: You only care about specific variants and match is cleaner than if let . This is covered by the built-in lint non_exhaustive_omitted_patterns which you can enable on your code. Use context strings to clarify assertions While some assertions are self-explanatory, many benefit from additional context that clarifies why an assertion is expected to hold, or what caused it to be violated. Use the optional format string argument for assert! to convey this context. You should always consider adding context, but particularly in the following situations: If you’re thinking of adding a comment to the assertion. Use a format string instead: It has the benefit that it will appear in logs. If you expect failing assertions to be seen by users. In this case, a human-readable explanation is more helpful than a Rust expression. If logging a value helps in understanding why the assertion failed. Cite as limitações e a data/jurisdição quando forem relevantes.", "response": "Padrões de qualidade e Lei Geral do Licenciamento Ambiental Skip to content Ambiente Jurídico Padrões de qualidade ambiental e Lei Geral do Licenciamento Ambiental Talden Farias 13 de setembro de 2026, 17h48 Ambiental O artigo 225 da Constituição de 1988 assegura o direito ao meio ambiente equilibrado, enquanto o artigo 170, VI, determina que a ordem econômica observe a defesa do meio ambiente, inclusive mediante tratamento diferenciado conforme o impacto ambiental das atividades econômicas. É nesse ponto de encontro entre proteção ambiental e desenvolvimento que se situa o princípio do limite, segundo o qual toda atividade humana produz alguma alteração no meio ambiente. Por isso, o Direito Ambiental não trabalha com a noção de impacto zero, mas com a distinção entre impactos juridicamente aceitáveis e níveis de degradação incompatíveis com a qualidade ambiental que o ordenamento pretende assegurar. Os padrões de qualidade ambiental transformam essa escolha em parâmetros técnicos e jurídicos mensuráveis, permitindo que o poder público controle emissões, efluentes, ruídos, resíduos e outras formas de pressão sobre o meio receptor. Spacca Essa sistemática foi instituída pela Política Nacional do Meio Ambiente — PNMA (Lei 6.938/1981), cujo objetivo é a preservação, a melhoria e a recuperação da qualidade ambiental, e que inclui entre seus instrumentos o estabelecimento de padrões de qualidade ambiental, a avaliação de impactos e o licenciamento das atividades efetiva ou potencialmente poluidoras (artigo 9º, I, III e IV), considerando poluição a degradação que lance matérias ou energia em desacordo com os padrões ambientais estabelecidos (artigo 3º, III). Logo, os padrões constituem o conteúdo material do licenciamento ambiental, servindo como parâmetro para auferir a viabilidade do empreendimento, definir tecnologias e medidas de controle, estabelecer condicionantes e verificar, durante a instalação e a operação, se o nível de intervenção permanece juridicamente admissível. Nessa perspectiva, os padrões desdobram-se em três planos: a qualidade do meio receptor (água, ar, solo, ruído, balneabilidade), os limites de emissão ou de lançamento das fontes poluidoras, e os padrões de desempenho tecnológico, que exigem determinada tecnologia ou eficiência mínima de controle e que a própria LGLA passou a incentivar no seu artigo 15. É a lógica que aparece, por exemplo, nos padrões de qualidade do ar (Resolução Conama 506/2024) e nas regras de enquadramento dos corpos de água e lançamento de efluentes (Resolução Conama 357/2005 e a norma do Conama de setembro de 2026, que revogou a Resolução 430/2011). A PNMA atribuiu ao Conama a competência para estabelecer normas, critérios e padrões para o licenciamento de atividades efetiva ou potencialmente poluidoras e para o controle e a manutenção da qualidade do meio ambiente (artigo 8º, I e VII). O Decreto 99.274/1990 (artigo 7º, I e VI) reproduz essa atribuição e permite, no artigo 14, que estados, Distrito Federal e municípios regionalizem as medidas do Sisnama mediante normas supletivas e complementares, observada a legislação federal. O mesmo decreto relaciona diretamente licença e desempenho ambiental, pois o artigo 18 determina a redução de atividades geradoras de poluição para manter emissões, efluentes e resíduos dentro dos limites estipulados, ao passo que o artigo 19, III, condiciona a licença de operação (LO) à verificação do funcionamento dos equipamentos de controle de poluição. A Resolução Conama 237/1997 definiu licença ambiental como o ato que estabelece condições, restrições e medidas de controle e permitiu, no artigo 12, §1º, procedimentos simplificados para atividades de pequeno potencial de impacto ambiental. É importante separar duas discussões historicamente mal compreendidas. Uma coisa é a competência do Conama para editar normas técnicas, critérios e padrões nacionais de proteção ambiental, e outra é a repartição da competência administrativa para licenciar. A Resolução 237/1997 tratou também desse segundo tema, mas a definição de qual ente federativo licencia não poderia ficar a cargo de resolução administrativa, pois o artigo 23, parágrafo único, da Constituição exigia lei complementar para tanto. Por isso, o assunto foi disciplinado pela Lei Complementar 140/2011 (LC 140), que regulamentou a cooperação administrativa e consagrou a regra do licenciamento por um único ente federativo, sem eliminar a atuação supletiva e subsidiária prevista na própria lei. A constitucionalidade dessa lei foi reconhecida pelo STF no julgamento da ADI 4.747 , que conferiu interpretação conforme aos artigos 14, §4º, e 17, §3º, para preservar a atuação supletiva diante de omissão, mora desproporcional ou insuficiência da tutela fiscalizatória. Ou seja, a racionalização da competência administrativa ambiental não pode suprimir o dever comum de proteção ambiental, nem autorizar um desfazimento do piso nacional de tutela. A Lei Geral do Licenciamento Ambiental — LGLA (Lei 15.190/2025) não revogou os artigos 8º, I e VII, e 9º, I, da PNMA, nem retirou do Conama a competência para editar padrões nacionais de qualidade ambiental. Os artigos 1º e 2º instituem que o licenciamento é orientado pela prevenção do dano, pelo desenvolvimento sustentável, pela avaliação de impactos, pela eficácia, eficiência e efetividade na gestão ambiental e pela cooperação federativa. Os artigos 4º a 26 disciplinam o enquadramento, as licenças, os planos de controle e monitoramento, a renovação, as hipóteses de não sujeição, a simplificação e a LAC, além das condicionantes fixadas conforme a magnitude dos impactos; os artigos 28 a 31 disciplinam os estudos ambientais; e os artigos 35, 41, 57, 59 e 65 reforçam informação, acompanhamento, responsabilização técnica e reação à degradação da qualidade ambiental. Uma das principais inovações, e objeto de polêmicas, está nos artigos 3º, XXXV e XXXVI, 4º, §1º, e 18, §1º. A LGLA permite que o ente federativo competente estabeleça critérios de porte e potencial poluidor, defina as tipologias sujeitas ao licenciamento e escolha o procedimento e o estudo ambiental a partir de localização, natureza, porte e potencial poluidor. A descentralização é coerente com o federalismo e com as diferentes realidades ambientais do país, mas não pode produzir ilhas regulatórias em que a mesma carga poluidora seja considerada ambientalmente aceitável em um estado e incompatível com a saúde ou o ecossistema em outro sem justificativa técnico-científica. A autonomia dos entes federativos incide sobre o exercício de suas competências e sobre a suplementação normativa, mas precisa conviver com os padrões nacionais mínimos editados no âmbito do Sisnama, de modo a assegurar um piso de proteção que não possa ser erodido por escolhas regulatórias aleatórias. LAC (Licença por adesão e compromisso) revela bem essa tensão O artigo 22 da LGLA passou a admitir a LAC para empreendimentos simultaneamente de pequeno ou médio porte e baixo ou médio potencial poluidor, desde que sejam previamente conhecidas as características gerais da região, as condições de instalação e operação, os impactos da tipologia e as medidas de controle, além das exclusões e vedações supervenientes introduzidas pela Lei 15.300/2025. A ampliação para a faixa intermediária constitui uma escolha legislativa relevante e discutível, cuja constitucionalidade será examinada pelo STF. Isso não significa, porém, que a LAC possa autorizar o descumprimento de padrões de emissão ou de qualidade do corpo receptor. A simplificação é e deverá ser sempre meramente procedimental, nunca material. Se a técnica ou o processo produtivo não forem capazes de manter a atividade dentro dos padrões aplicáveis, estará ausente o pressuposto para a própria regularidade ambiental da operação. A mesma distinção vale para as hipóteses de dispensa ou de não sujeição ao licenciamento previstas nos artigos 8º, 9º e 10 da LGLA. A não exigência de licença ambiental não equivale a dispensar o cumprimento da legislação ambiental. O artigo 9º, §§2º e 3º, preserva a fiscalização, as sanções e outras autorizações e obrigações ambientais. O artigo 10, §4º, ao tratar do saneamento, articula a autoridade outorgante de recursos hídricos e o órgão ambiental para definir ou revisar a classe do corpo de água conforme os usos preponderantes — evidenciando que a simplificação procedimental não elimina a disciplina material da qualidade hídrica. A consequência é que a atividade não sujeita a licenciamento continua submetida aos padrões de qualidade, aos limites de emissão, à fiscalização e à responsabilidade ambiental; caso lance matéria ou energia em desacordo com os padrões estabelecidos, incidirá o conceito de poluição da PNMA, bem como as sanções cabíveis. Toda hipótese de dispensa construída em bloco, por categoria econômica ou setor de atividade, e não a partir da avaliação técnica do potencial poluidor de cada caso concreto, subverte a lógica constitucional do controle prévio e tende a subordinar o critério técnico a pressões políticas e setoriais. Aliás, o STF possui jurisprudência consolidada a respeito da inconstitucionalidade da inexigência de licença ambiental para atividades efetiva ou potencialmente poluidoras. A LGLA não construiu um sistema baseado apenas na emissão formal da licença, pois esta é apenas o mecanismo pelo qual a administração pública exige o cumprimento dos padrões de qualidade ambiental. O artigo 14 estabelece a hierarquia entre prevenção, mitigação e compensação e exige nexo causal e proporcionalidade das condicionantes, o que guarda consonância com o artigo 170, VI, da Constituição Federal. O artigo 15 cria incentivos para o empreendedor que adote tecnologia, programa de gestão ou outra medida capaz de superar os padrões e critérios legalmente estabelecidos, o que associa simplificação a desempenho ambiental superior. Os artigos 7º e 16 formam um regime de estabilidade dinâmica, pois a renovação considera a efetividade das ações de controle e monitoramento e exige que a legislação aplicável não tenha sido alterada, e as condicionantes podem ser revistas diante de impactos imprevistos, alterações relevantes ou inefetividade técnica.
